findings.confidence_reason: Unanchored StartsWith confirmed at line 138; localhost.evil.com would indeed match, but exploit is DEBUG-only and needs attacker-controlled DNS plus a settings value pointing at a localhost-prefixed hostname - technically real, practically contrived.

findings.title: Antiforgery runs before HTTPS redirection; cookie Secure flag dependent on forwarded-proto trust
findings.description: Program.cs orders UseAntiforgery (line 24) before UseHttpsRedirection (line 26) - the inverse of the standard template order. Unsafe requests arriving over plaintext HTTP are processed (form read + token validation) by the antiforgery middleware before any redirect, and the subsequent 307-preserving redirect means the original POST (credentials/antiforgery token) was already transmitted in cleartext. Related: the auth cookie is configured with only ExpireTimeSpan (WebApp/Extensions/Extensions.cs:71) and no explicit SecurePolicy; the default SameAsRequest marks the session cookie non-Secure whenever the request scheme is seen as http. There is no UseForwardedHeaders/ForwardedHeadersOptions in ServiceDefaults at all; forwarded-proto handling is instead switched on for every project by the AppHost env injection ASPNETCORE_FORWARDEDHEADERS_ENABLED=true (src/eShop.AppHost/Extensions.cs:34-37), which trusts only loopback peers by default - leaving proto/cookie-flag correctness hostage to whether the real TLS terminator is loopback.
findings.exploit_scenario: On a network path where the WebApp HTTP listener is reachable, a victim's browser POSTs the login/checkout form over http; antiforgery validates it and the 307 re-send leaks the payload, while the issued session cookie lacks Secure and can ride subsequent http requests where an observer recovers it.
findings.recommendation: Move UseHttpsRedirection ahead of UseAntiforgery (right after exception handling), set Cookie.SecurePolicy = Always on the auth cookie, and configure explicit ForwardedHeadersOptions (AllowedHosts, KnownProxies) in ServiceDefaults rather than relying on the apphost env switch.
findings.confidence_reason: All cited facts verified (ordering, cookie options, env-injected forwarded headers), but exploitation hinges on a plaintext HTTP listener being reachable in the deployed topology - plaintext-transport hardening issue.

findings.title: Webhook subscription tokens stored in plaintext in PostgreSQL
findings.description: WebhookSubscription.Token (WebhookSubscription.cs:11) is persisted as-is by WebhooksContext (Infrastructure/WebhooksContext.cs:14-18 maps only indexes; no value converter/encryption), so all users' webhook secrets sit in cleartext in the webhooksdb Postgres store and in any backups. Defense-in-depth issue: anyone with DB read access (SQL injection elsewhere, backup leak, insider) gains every registered webhook secret, enabling spoofed deliveries to receivers that enforce token checks.
findings.exploit_scenario: Compromise of the webhooksdb database (or a leaked backup dump) yields every subscription token directly from the Subscriptions table, which is then replayed against the corresponding DestUrls' receivers.
findings.recommendation: Store tokens encrypted at rest (application-level envelope encryption with a KMS-held key, or hash+pepper when only verification is needed) rather than raw strings.
findings.confidence_reason: Confirmed Token persisted verbatim with no encryption/value converter - legitimate CWE-312 defense-in-depth finding, but impact is limited to replaying webhook secrets a DB reader could mostly observe anyway.

findings.title: OpenAPI documents served unauthenticated in all environments; docs advertise deprecated implicit OAuth flow
findings.description: UseDefaultOpenApi maps app.MapOpenApi() (line 24) whenever an "OpenApi" section exists - with no environment gate and no RequireAuthorization; only the Scalar UI is Development-gated (lines 26-42). Consumers ship the section in appsettings.json that is deployed with production images (Ordering.API/appsettings.json:9-22, Catalog.API/appsettings.json:8, Webhooks.API/appsettings.json:9), so /openapi/v1.json is live in prod, exposing the full route inventory, scope names, and the Identity URL. Additionally the SecuritySchemeDefinitionsTransformer (src/eShop.ServiceDefaults/OpenApiOptionsExtensions.cs:171-184) publishes an OAuth2 Implicit flow (with a TODO at line 176 admitting it should be code+PKCE), advertising to outsiders both a weaker flow and the internal IdP endpoints ($"{identityUrlExternal}/connect/authorize", line 179). Impact is recon assistance rather than direct compromise.
findings.exploit_scenario: An external attacker reaching any eShop API through the ingress requests /openapi/v1.json and enumerates every internal route, expected auth scopes, and the internal identity hostname, then targets undocumented mutation endpoints directly.
findings.recommendation: Gate MapOpenApi behind IsDevelopment() (matching the Scalar branch) or an authorization policy, and replace the implicit-flow scheme definition with authorization code + PKCE.
findings.confidence_reason: All claims verified (ungated MapOpenApi in prod-shipped configs, dev-gated Scalar only, implicit-flow TODO) - genuine recon-aid disclosure but low-impact route/spec enumeration, not data compromise.

findings.title: RequireHttpsMetadata=false plus http:// Authority enables MITM-forged IdP discovery -> fleet-wide token forgery
findings.description: Line 38 sets options.Authority = identityUrl and line 39 sets options.RequireHttpsMetadata = false; the canonical config comment (line 17) and Aspire wiring use "http://identity" in the http launch profile, so discovery document and JWKS would be fetched over plaintext. Any network-positioned attacker (compromised pod, ARP/DNS spoof on the container network, hostile DHCP) can intercept the /.well-known/openid-configuration + jwks requests and serve their own keys, then mint JWTs with iss == identityUrl, which passes ValidIssuers (line 46) and - per F-024 - needs no valid audience. The identical weakness exists in the WebApp OIDC client (src/WebApp/Extensions/Extensions.cs:75 Authority = identityUrl and line 82 RequireHttpsMetadata = false), additionally exposing the authorization-code exchange (client_secret sent in cleartext to the spoofed token endpoint). Counterweights found during scoring: AppHost defaults to the https launch profile (http is the opt-in local-dev mode), and exploitation requires an attacker network position inside the deployment.
findings.exploit_scenario: Attacker with a foothold on the cluster network spoofs DNS for "identity" while a deployment runs the http profile; the next service or WebApp OIDC handshake fetches attacker JWKS; attacker issues a signed JWT with iss=http://identity and any sub/role claims, gaining access to Ordering/Basket/Webhooks APIs as any user.
findings.recommendation: Set RequireHttpsMetadata = true unconditionally in the shared library (or gate strictly on an explicit opt-in env for local dev), and default Authority to https in all deployment config.
findings.confidence_reason: RequireHttpsMetadata=false confirmed but AppHost defaults to the https launch profile (http is opt-in local-dev), and exploit needs a MITM position on the internal network plus non-default http config - dev-config-bleed hardening gap.

findings.title: Forged OrderStartedIntegrationEvent deletes any user's basket keyed on attacker-controlled UserId
findings.description: The handler's sole action is `repository.DeleteBasketAsync(@event.UserId)` (line 14), where UserId comes straight from the deserialized JSON body; RedisBasketRepository maps it directly to key "/basket/{id}" (src/Basket.API/Repositories/RedisBasketRepository.cs:13-21) and deletes it. The message enters via RabbitMQEventBus with no authentication of the publisher, and there is no verification that a corresponding order was actually created in Ordering.API, nor dedup. The event's UserId equals the authenticated username used as the basket key. Reach requires broker access. (Related: F-013 reaches the same sink from the HTTP API via client-controlled UserId.)
findings.exploit_scenario: An actor connected to the broker publishes {"UserId":"victim@example.com"} with routing key OrderStartedIntegrationEvent; the victim's Redis basket ("/basket/victim@example.com") is deleted, silently emptying their shopping cart before checkout.
findings.recommendation: Make deletion conditional and verifiable (e.g., include an order Id that Basket.API validates exists via Ordering.API, or have Basket.API query recent OrderStarted events in the outbox), and/or sign events so subscribers can reject unauthenticated publishers.
findings.confidence_reason: DeleteBasketAsync keyed purely on event UserId is confirmed and wired via AddSubscription, but the broker-access precondition and low blast radius (cart wipe) make it borderline noise in triage without an internal foothold.

findings.title: Catalog "stock validation" handler confirms stock for arbitrary OrderIds and silently treats missing products as in-stock
findings.description: The handler reads OrderId and OrderStockItems straight from the event (lines 15-25), looks each ProductId up in CatalogItems, and builds ConfirmOrderStock items only for products it found; products missing from the catalog are silently dropped. The decision at lines 27-29 (`confirmedOrderStockItems.Any(c => !c.HasStock) ? Rejected : Confirmed`) therefore defaults to OrderStockConfirmedIntegrationEvent for @event.OrderId whenever: (a) no product id matches (empty list -> false), (b) every requested Units fits available stock, or (c) Units is negative (>= comparison trivially passes). It then saves and publishes through the event bus (lines 31-32). Nothing verifies the order exists, that Ordering.API actually put it in AwaitingValidation, or that the item list corresponds to the real order lines. Reach requires broker publish access (internal trust boundary).
findings.exploit_scenario: Actor with broker access publishes OrderStatusChangedToAwaitingValidationIntegrationEvent{"OrderId":42,"OrderStockItems":[{"ProductId":999999,"Units":1}]} (nonexistent product) for a submitted order; Catalog replies OrderStockConfirmed for order 42, and combined with the grace-period event the order reaches StockConfirmed despite never having valid stock checks.
findings.recommendation: Reject events whose OrderId cannot be correlated to a known awaiting-validation order; treat unknown ProductIds as a rejection (fail-closed) rather than omission; reject non-positive Units.
findings.confidence_reason: Default-confirm logic is real (skipped products -> empty list -> Any()==false -> Confirmed; negative Units passes), but exploiting it requires forging integration events on the internal RabbitMQ bus - speculative business-logic weakness without broker compromise.

findings.title: android:allowBackup="true" backs up plaintext Preferences (OIDC authority, gateway URLs, client secret) enabling settings-tamper restore
findings.description: AndroidManifest.xml line 3 sets android:allowBackup="true" with no fullBackupContent/dataExtractionRules exclusions. SettingsService keeps security-routing data in plaintext Preferences (SettingsService.cs:55-125): url_base (OIDC Authority consumed at IdentityService.cs:137), url_shopping/url_basket/url_orders, ClientId/ClientSecret (SettingsService.cs:79-89, DefaultClientSecret "secret" at line 15), and UseMocks. ADB/cloud backup therefore contains the full security routing table in cleartext (tokens themselves are in SecureStorage ciphertext, which is properly key-protected). Restoring a doctored backup - or any rooted-device modification - repoints the app to an attacker-controlled IdP/gateway, converging with F-036 into credential capture and token exfiltration.
findings.exploit_scenario: Attacker briefly gains ADB/device access (shared device, malicious charger/kiosk scenarios), extracts the auto-backup, rewrites url_base to their IdP, restores it; the victim's next sign-in authenticates on the attacker's page and the refresh token lands with the attacker.
findings.recommendation: Set allowBackup=false (or dataExtractionRules excluding SharedPreferences), and/or store endpoint/authority configuration in SecureStorage with an integrity check (HMAC) before use as OIDC Authority.
findings.confidence_reason: allowBackup=true with no exclusions and plaintext Preferences verified (tokens correctly in SecureStorage), but exploitation needs prior ADB/root/restore access and merely converges on F-036's tampering - real config hygiene, low practical impact.

findings.title: iOS NSAllowsLocalNetworking=true permits cleartext to LAN hosts where the default gateway endpoints live
findings.description: Platforms/iOS/Info.plist lines 33-37 set NSAllowsLocalNetworking=true (no debug gating). The app's default shopping/basket/orders endpoints are `http://{base}:...` (SettingsViewModel.cs:58,63,68, with base = "10.0.2.2" on Android or "localhost" elsewhere, line 16) - on iOS the base is localhost-class, so the LAN-cleartext exposure requires the user to reconfigure endpoints to another LAN host. Basket gRPC attaches the access token as a header (BasketService.cs:125,132-137), so LAN plaintext exposes bearer tokens to on-path attackers.
findings.exploit_scenario: User on a hostile Wi-Fi runs the release iOS build configured against a local-network gateway (requires reconfiguration from the shipped default); attacker performs ARP spoofing on the LAN, receives the http gRPC/REST traffic, and extracts the `authorization: Bearer` access token for replay against the BFF.
findings.recommendation: Ship https:// gateway defaults, drop the NSAllowsLocalNetworking exception from release, or at minimum refuse non-https endpoint values for anything except a DEBUG configuration.
findings.confidence_reason: NSAllowsLocalNetworking=true confirmed and not debug-gated, but the non-Android default gateway is localhost (10.0.2.2 is Android-only), so on-device LAN cleartext requires the user to reconfigure endpoints - prerequisite-heavy.

findings.title: Consumer swallows all handler exceptions and acknowledges every message - poison events cause silent event loss
findings.description: OnMessageReceived wraps ProcessEvent in try/catch (lines 159-175): any deserialization failure or handler exception is only logged (line 172) and the message is unconditionally acknowledged (line 180, "Even on exception we take the message off the queue", no DLX per comment at 177-179). Untrusted broker input triggers this path trivially: a malformed body for any bound routing key throws inside JsonSerializer.Deserialize (line 215); wrong-typed fields throw inside handlers. Because the message is acked, the event is permanently consumed with no dead-lettering and no retry, while operators only see a Warning. An actor with broker access can deterministically suppress legitimate business events (interleaving poison copies on the same routing key, since queue delivery is FIFO per channel) - e.g. mask a real OrderStatusChangedToPaidIntegrationEvent so stock is never deducted while Ordering marks the order Paid.
findings.exploit_scenario: Enqueue {"OrderId":42,"OrderStockItems":[{"ProductId":1,"Units":"x"}]} with routing key OrderStatusChangedToPaidIntegrationEvent just before the genuine event for order 42; the poison message throws, is acked, and (depending on ordering) the stock deduction vanishes with only a log line as evidence.
findings.recommendation: Negative-ack with a Dead Letter Exchange for deserialization/handler failures, cap retries, and alert on dead-letter volume. Separate deserialization failures from handler failures; do not ack messages that failed transient processing.
findings.confidence_reason: Catch-log-ack behavior verified verbatim including the DLX comment, but this is an acknowledged reliability trade-off (missing DLX hardening), and attacker capability adds little beyond what broker access already confers.

findings.title: Missing "Identity" config section silently disables all authentication and authorization for a service
findings.description: Lines 24-28: if the Identity configuration section does not exist, AddDefaultAuthentication returns early - skipping both services.AddAuthentication().AddJwtBearer(...) (line 33) and services.AddAuthorization() (line 52). There is no log, exception, or startup warning. In ASP.NET Core minimal hosting, UseAuthentication/UseAuthorization middleware are only auto-inserted when the corresponding services are registered; with neither registered, the [Authorize]/RequireAuthorization() metadata that Ordering.API attaches to all order endpoints would not be enforced. IMPORTANT scoring caveat: shipped Ordering/Basket appsettings DO define an Identity section (Audience), so with a merely missing Identity__Url env var the GetRequiredValue("Url") call throws at startup - fail-closed/loud rather than silently anonymous. The silent path requires deliberately stripping the Identity section from appsettings as well. A sibling pattern exists in the OpenAPI extension (OpenApi.Extensions.cs:19-22), which silently drops the auth security scheme when Identity is absent.
findings.exploit_scenario: A deployment profile or chart that removes the whole Identity:* configuration (section and env) launches ordering-api cleanly with zero auth handlers; unauthenticated clients POST to /api/orders/* and get order operations processed anonymously, and monitoring shows no anomaly.
findings.recommendation: Make the missing-section case fail fast (throw InvalidOperationException) or register an explicit DenyAnonymous authorization fallback plus an error-level log; never return a "works but unprotected" service silently.
findings.confidence_reason: Early-return/no-logging is real, but shipped Ordering/Basket appsettings define the Identity section so a missing Identity__Url env var crashes loudly via GetRequiredValue instead of silently disabling auth - the described scenario needs an additional config-stripping step.

findings.title: Hardcoded OIDC client secret "secret" compiled into the client and stored in plaintext Preferences
findings.description: SettingsService.cs line 15 defines DefaultClientSecret = "secret" (used as the OidcClientOptions ClientSecret at IdentityService.cs:139, and passed as Basic auth credentials through RequestProvider.cs:139-152). The value ships inside the app binary and defaults into plaintext Preferences (SettingsService.cs:85-89), so every APK/IPA holder can extract it. As a native public client the secret provides no real protection (and OidcClient 6.x already uses PKCE), but its presence encourages server-side acceptance of confidential-client flows from a public client.
findings.exploit_scenario: Attacker decompiles the app, recovers client_id "maui"/client_secret "secret", and uses them to impersonate the official client against the identity provider (e.g., requesting tokens for arbitrary redirect URIs the IdP tolerates).
findings.recommendation: Remove the client secret from the native client entirely (pure public client + PKCE), or move to DPoP/mTLS-bound tokens; never send Basic-auth credentials from the app.
findings.confidence_reason: Secret verifiably compiled in, but it is the obvious demo value in a native public OIDC client where a secret confers no security boundary anyway; technically true yet nearly impact-free given PKCE.

findings.title: webapp confidential client disables PKCE on the authorization-code flow
findings.description: Config.cs:90 sets `RequirePkce = false` for the "webapp" client while AllowOfflineAccess=true (line 88) issues long-lived refresh tokens. Without PKCE, the authorization code is not bound to a verifier, so an interceptor of the code can redeem it - facilitated here because the client secret is hardcoded and public (F-020/F-018). The redirect_uri https://{WebAppClient}/signin-oidc is registered, so code theft plus the known secret yields a usable token exchange.
findings.exploit_scenario: Attacker obtains an authorization code for webapp from a leaked Referer header, browser history, or proxy logs; redeems it at /connect/token with client_secret=secret (no code_verifier needed) and receives the user's access and refresh tokens.
findings.recommendation: Set RequirePkce = true for all code-flow clients (Duende 7 supports PKCE for confidential clients; it removes reliance on secret-alone binding of the code).
findings.confidence_reason: Confirmed RequirePkce=false with AllowOfflineAccess=true on the webapp confidential client, but for confidential clients this is a missing-hardening/weak-default issue whose exploitation additionally needs code interception plus the shared secret.

findings.title: PAN masking runs before validation and throws unhandled for CardNumber shorter than 4 chars or null
findings.description: `request.CardNumber.Substring(request.CardNumber.Length - 4)` (OrdersApi.cs:140) throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException for length 0-3 (startIndex negative) and `.Length` throws NullReferenceException when CardNumber is absent. The FluentValidation rule that would reject such input (`CardNumber.NotEmpty().Length(12,19)`, CreateOrderCommandValidator.cs:11) executes only later inside the MediatR pipeline, so malformed card numbers reach this line raw and bubble up as an unhandled 500 (only mitigated by ProblemDetails middleware).
findings.exploit_scenario: POST /api/orders with "CardNumber": "" (or omitted) and an otherwise valid x-requestid -> unhandled exception, HTTP 500, spammed to fill error-tracking/log volumes with stack traces rather than a clean 400.
findings.recommendation: Guard the masking (e.g. only mask when length >= 4, else route to validation) and/or perform schema-level validation on the request DTO before constructing the command.
findings.confidence_reason: Mechanism is real (Substring/NRE fires before FluentValidation; non-nullable record params aren't enforced by STJ binding), but impact is only an unhandled 500 - a robustness bug, not an exploitable security issue.

findings.title: Order-status handlers log full integration events including buyer name and identity GUID
findings.description: All six order-status event handlers log the whole event with structured logging, e.g. `logger.LogInformation("Handling integration event: {IntegrationEventId} - ({@IntegrationEvent})", @event.Id, @event)` (Cancelled handler line 12; same pattern in the AwaitingValidation handler line 12 and the other four). The events carry `BuyerName` and `BuyerIdentityGuid` (OrderStatusChangedToCancelledIntegrationEvent.cs:9-10), so the buyer's display name and stable identity GUID land in application logs/telemetry on every status transition, aggregated across the entire customer base. The bus payload is NOT rendered in the UI (handlers only trigger a refresh) - no XSS path exists here.
findings.exploit_scenario: No direct browser-exploitable path; impact is privacy/compliance: log access or log exfiltration exposes per-buyer name-identity correlation and shopping/order lifecycle metadata for all customers.
findings.recommendation: Log only `@event.Id` and the event type name; exclude BuyerName and BuyerIdentityGuid from log serialization (or hash the identity GUID).
findings.confidence_reason: Accurately reported - handlers log the full event including BuyerName/BuyerIdentityGuid at Information level; genuine PII-in-logs/compliance issue with no XSS path, but pure privacy hygiene.

findings.title: OIDC confidential client secret hardcoded as "secret" with HTTPS metadata enforcement disabled
findings.description: WebhookClient's OpenIdConnect handler hardcodes options.ClientSecret = "secret" (Extensions/Extensions.cs:54) and options.RequireHttpsMetadata = false (line 58). The client secret is a committed credential for the confidential 'webhooksclient' client; RequireHttpsMetadata=false additionally permits discovery/token endpoints over plain HTTP if the Authority URL is misconfigured, exposing code-for-token exchanges to interception.
findings.exploit_scenario: Anyone with repo access knows the client secret for webhooksclient and can attempt its own authorization-code exchange against the identity provider if network reachability exists; a MITM on the HTTP metadata fetch can serve attacker-controlled OIDC endpoints to steal authorization codes.
findings.recommendation: Load the client secret from configuration/secret store (key vault, env), and set RequireHttpsMetadata = true for non-development environments.
findings.confidence_reason: Both facts verified (ClientSecret="secret" at line 54, RequireHttpsMetadata=false at line 58) - committed public sample credential, but sample-app context and dev-only HTTPS relaxation make it a low-severity hardening finding.

findings.title: Forged paid/shipped events are fanned out to all webhook subscribers with valid tokens and attacker-controlled payload
findings.description: The handlers dispatch every received event verbatim: `new WebhookData(WebhookType.OrderPaid, @event)` (line 14) then `sender.SendAll(subscriptions, whook)` (line 16); WebhookData serializes the whole event to JSON (src/Webhooks.API/Model/WebhookData.cs:13) and WebhooksSender POSTs it to every registered DestUrl with the subscriber's secret token header (src/Webhooks.API/Services/WebhooksSender.cs:13-33). Because consume-side events are unauthenticated (same path as F-034), an actor can fabricate OrderStatusChangedToPaid/Shipped events - the event embeds BuyerName, BuyerIdentityGuid and OrderId chosen by the sender - and cause all downstream integrators to receive authenticated-looking notifications carrying their own valid X-eshop-whtoken. Reach requires broker publish access; downstream impact depends on subscriber logic not in this repo.
findings.exploit_scenario: Actor forges OrderStatusChangedToShippedIntegrationEvent{"OrderId":999,"BuyerName":"x"}; every webhook subscriber's fulfilment/ERP automation treats it as genuine (token valid) and acts on a shipment that never occurred.
findings.recommendation: Sign outbound webhook payloads with a per-dispatcher signing key (HMAC) distinct from the subscriber token, and rate-limit/dedup dispatch per event Id; verify event authenticity before fan-out.
findings.confidence_reason: Verbatim fan-out of received events to subscribers with valid tokens is confirmed, but impact lives entirely downstream of speculative subscriber logic and still requires forged broker access.

findings.title: RabbitMQ and Redis are provisioned without explicit authentication parameters; network-adjacent callers can forge integration events and read/rewrite any basket
findings.description: AppHost provisions the event broker and cache without explicit user/password parameters: `builder.AddRabbitMQ("eventbus")` (AppHost.cs:10-11) and `builder.AddRedis("redis")` (AppHost.cs:9), and every service talks to them over plain AMQP/RESP. All automatic state transitions trust these channels: OrderProcessor polls the DB and publishes GracePeriodConfirmedIntegrationEvent(orderId) (src/OrderProcessor/Services/GracePeriodManagerService.cs:50-61), PaymentProcessor decides payment outcome and publishes OrderPaymentSucceededIntegrationEvent(@event.OrderId) (src/PaymentProcessor/.../OrderStatusChangedToStockConfirmedIntegrationEventHandler.cs:21-32) - the consumers apply status changes keyed only on the event payload's orderId. A workload (or SSRF-primed attacker) on the internal network can therefore publish fabricated events to advance/cancel any order, or connect to Redis to read/overwrite/delete every /basket/* document keyed by raw sub. Scoring caveat: Aspire's AddRabbitMQ typically generates a random password when none is supplied (guest/guest fallback only applies to bare-metal runs), and the vector presumes an internal-network foothold.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker who gains a foothold on any container in the app network connects to the broker (with whatever credentials Aspire generated, or guest/guest on a bare-metal run) and publishes an OrderPaymentSucceededIntegrationEvent with an arbitrary orderId, marking an unpaid order as Paid; similarly, speaking RESP to redis allows SET/DEL of any user's /basket/<sub> key if Redis is reachable unauthenticated.
findings.recommendation: Provision RabbitMQ with generated credentials (Aspire parameters) and Redis with a password/ACL, and restrict broker publishers to their exchange/queue permissions; consider signed integration events for state-transition topics.
findings.confidence_reason: Broker/cache-without-explicit-auth and trust-on-payload confirmed, but Aspire's AddRabbitMQ generates a random password when none is supplied (guest/guest claim shaky), AppHost is dev/ACA orchestration rather than hardened prod config, and the vector requires an existing internal-network foothold.

findings.title: AppHost forces ASPNETCORE_FORWARDEDHEADERS_ENABLED=true on all projects, enabling client-supplied X-Forwarded-* spoofing that bypasses an IP gate
findings.description: AddForwardedHeaders subscribes to BeforeStartEvent and sets ASPNETCORE_FORWARDEDHEADERS_ENABLED=true for every DotnetProjectResource (src/eShop.AppHost/Extensions.cs:26-45, AppHost.cs:6). Per ASP.NET Core documentation, this flag "uses settings designed for cloud environments and doesn't enable features such as the KnownProxies option" - i.e., the auto-injected forwarded-headers middleware processes X-Forwarded-For/Proto from remote clients, rewriting Connection.RemoteIpAddress and Request.Scheme. Several services are directly reachable without a proxy (identity-api `.WithExternalHttpEndpoints()`, src/eShop.AppHost/AppHost.cs:25-28). One concrete consumer of the spoofable value exists: Identity.API's DiagnosticsController gates on `RemoteIpAddress in {127.0.0.1, ::1, LocalIpAddress}` (src/Identity.API/Quickstart/Diagnostics/DiagnosticsController.cs:13-17). Scoring caveat: the forwarded-headers default processes only X-Forwarded-For/Proto, and the bypassed gate merely shows callers their own auth artifacts.
findings.exploit_scenario: Authenticated attacker sends GET https://identity-api/diagnostics with header `X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1` directly to the service's exposed HTTP endpoint; RemoteIpAddress is rewritten to 127.0.0.1 and the "local only" diagnostics page renders instead of 404 - showing the caller their own claim payload.
findings.recommendation: Set ForwardedHeadersOptions.KnownProxies/KnownNetworks to the actual proxy IPs instead of blanket env-var enablement, or drop the IP gate in favor of an explicit config flag for the diagnostics endpoint.
findings.confidence_reason: Mechanism verified (env var set for all projects, identity-api has external HTTP endpoints, DiagnosticsController gates on RemoteIpAddress), but the forwarded-headers default processes only X-Forwarded-For/Proto and the bypassed gate merely shows callers their own auth artifacts - negligible concrete impact.

findings.title: CI actions pinned to mutable major tags; unpinned npm global install in workflow
findings.description: All four workflows reference actions by mutable tag rather than commit SHA: actions/checkout@v4 (playwright.yml:22, pr-validation.yml:23, pr-validation-maui.yml:23, markdownlint.yml:17), actions/setup-dotnet@v3/@v4 (pr-validation.yml:25, playwright.yml:23, pr-validation-maui.yml:25), actions/setup-node@v4 (playwright.yml:26, markdownlint.yml:19), actions/upload-artifact@v4 (playwright.yml:39). markdownlint.yml:25 also runs `npm i -g markdownlint-cli` fetching the latest package at run time. No workflow uses pull_request_target and no secrets are passed to PR builds (checked), which limits fork exposure; the residual risk is upstream action/package compromise executing in-repo CI with the workflow token.
findings.exploit_scenario: A compromised actions/checkout or markdownlint-cli release runs attacker code inside the eShop CI runner with the GITHUB_TOKEN and repo checkout, enabling artifact/build tampering or secret exfiltration of any secrets added to the workflows later.
findings.recommendation: Pin actions to full commit SHAs; use a lockfile-based npm invocation with `npm ci` in a project directory instead of global latest.
findings.confidence_reason: Accurately reported (mutable tags, global npm install), but textbook missing-hardening-only: no pull_request_target and no secrets exposed to PR builds, so the residual theoretical upstream-compromise risk is defense-in-depth advice.

findings.title: CI uploads Playwright report artifact containing authenticated-session traces for 30 days
findings.description: playwright.config.ts:5 stores the authenticated storage state at `playwright/.auth/user.json` (gitignored, good) and line 27 enables `trace: 'on-first-retry'` with `retries: 2` on CI (line 17). playwright.yml:39-44 uploads `playwright-report/` with `if: always()` and 30-day retention. Retried tests attach their trace.zip to the uploaded HTML report; Playwright traces embed network request/response data (including Cookie/Authorization headers of the logged-in 'bob' session created with the Pass123$ credentials at playwright.yml:37-38) and authenticated page snapshots.
findings.exploit_scenario: Anyone with read access to the (public) repository downloads the `playwright-report` artifact and extracts session cookies/tokens for the CI-created bob account from embedded traces. Scoring caveat: the app-under-test is spun up fresh per job on localhost via the AppHost webServer, so captured tokens only ever authenticate against an ephemeral instance, and the seeded credentials are already public in the repo.
findings.recommendation: Disable trace upload or scrub network data in CI, use throwaway credentials, and shorten artifact retention; do not upload reports on retries that contain captured traffic.
findings.confidence_reason: Facts verified (artifact upload with if:always()/30d, trace on retry, auth storage state), but the exploit chain collapses - tokens only authenticate against the ephemeral CI instance and the credentials are already public; artifact-hygiene nit.

findings.title: EventBus connection string falls back to amqp://localhost with implicit guest/guest credentials
findings.description: Checked-in configs ship `"EventBus": "amqp://localhost"` with no credentials: Basket.API/appsettings.json:15, Catalog.API/appsettings.json:19, Ordering.API/appsettings.json:24, OrderProcessor/appsettings.json:9, PaymentProcessor/appsettings.json:9, Webhooks.API/appsettings.json:24. RabbitMqDependencyInjectionExtensions.cs:21 resolves this connection name via `builder.AddRabbitMQClient(connectionName)`; when the orchestrator-supplied connection string is missing (container run outside Aspire), the client connects to `localhost` with RabbitMQ.Client's default guest/guest credentials. In deployed shape the real credentials are Aspire-generated (AppHost.cs:10), so this is a misconfiguration path rather than a direct exposure.
findings.exploit_scenario: An operator deploys a service container without the orchestrator-provided EventBus connection string; the service silently attempts guest/guest access, and if it lands on any reachable broker permitting guest it publishes/consumes events on the wrong broker unauthenticated.
findings.recommendation: Fail fast when the EventBus connection string is absent in non-development environments instead of falling back to localhost defaults.
findings.confidence_reason: Technically accurate reading, but it is the standard .NET local-dev default pattern - production runs via Aspire which injects real credentials, and a missing connection string fails closed (connect error) unless a separately-permissive broker is also misdeployed.

findings.title: AndroidManifest ships usesCleartextTraffic="true"; network_security_config carve-out allows cleartext to 10.0.2.2
findings.description: AndroidManifest.xml line 3 declares `android:usesCleartextTraffic="true"` together with `android:networkSecurityConfig="@xml/network_security_config"`. On API 24+ the NSC supersedes the manifest flag, so the effective policy (Resources/xml/network_security_config.xml:3-5) is: cleartext permitted only to 10.0.2.2 (includeSubdomains). Two residual exposures: (1) any traffic the app directs to 10.0.2.2 - the persisted default gateway endpoints (F-036) - is unauthenticated plaintext carrying the Bearer token; (2) the flag is inert-but-contradictory and reverts to global-cleartext semantics if the NSC is later removed. No <domain-config> pins or trust anchors are configured.
findings.exploit_scenario: Emulator-based flow: app talks to the host-side gateway at http://10.0.2.2:5221 with the Bearer token in headers; any process on the dev host (or a compromised emulator image) captures the token. On real devices the flag is currently neutralized by the NSC.
findings.recommendation: Remove android:usesCleartextTraffic (rely solely on the NSC), scope the 10.0.2.2 cleartext carve-out to a debug-only NSC variant, and consider certificate pinning the production gateways.
findings.confidence_reason: Both flags verified, but on API 24+ the network_security_config supersedes usesCleartextTraffic=true (making the flag inert) and the surviving carve-out is limited to 10.0.2.2 emulator-to-dev-host traffic - mostly noise.

findings.title: "throw-fake-exception" magic string in the message body suppresses all event processing
findings.description: Lines 163-166: any received message whose body contains the substring "throw-fake-exception" (case-insensitive) throws InvalidOperationException before ProcessEvent runs, so registered handlers are skipped entirely - and the message is still acked (line 180). This is a debugging trapdoor left in the production consume path; the trigger is fully attacker-controlled broker input. Scoring caveat: it only drops the message containing the string itself, and an actor with broker access can suppress events without it anyway.
findings.exploit_scenario: An actor with broker access publishes a valid-shaped OrderStartedIntegrationEvent body with the string embedded (or any message on any bound routing key, since the check precedes type resolution at line 192) to make a consumer drop exactly one legit event without deserialization noise.
findings.recommendation: Remove the check from production code or gate it behind an environment/feature flag enabled only in test deployments.
findings.confidence_reason: The "throw-fake-exception" string exists exactly as cited, but it only drops the message containing the string itself - an actor with broker access can suppress events without it, so it is intentional debug scaffolding, not a meaningful backdoor primitive.

findings.title: ExternalController.Challenge accepts arbitrary caller-supplied authentication scheme and later trusts it as the identity-provider label
findings.description: Challenge(string scheme, string returnUrl) (ExternalController.cs:34-57) puts the unvalidated `scheme` into AuthenticationProperties and challenges it directly (`return Challenge(props, scheme)`, line 56). During Callback, the same caller-chosen value is read back as the provider identity (line 151: `provider = result.Properties.Items["scheme"]`) and used for `FindByLoginAsync(provider, providerUserId)` (line 155) and `AddLoginAsync(user, new UserLoginInfo(provider, providerUserId, provider))` (line 213), i.e., account linking keyed on a request-controlled string. Currently dormant because Program.cs registers no external authentication handlers, so any challenge with an unknown scheme throws rather than misroutes.
findings.exploit_scenario: (Dormant precondition: at least one external provider registered.) Attacker initiates /External/Challenge?scheme=<schemeB>&returnUrl=... and the resulting ApplicationUserLogin is stored under an attacker-chosen provider label, enabling account-link confusion in FindByLoginAsync on subsequent logins.
findings.recommendation: Validate `scheme` against registered external providers (whitelist from IAuthenticationSchemeProvider.GetExternalAuthenticationSchemesAsync) before challenging, and derive `provider` from the authenticated result rather than the echoed Items value.
findings.confidence_reason: Flow accurately described but dormant - Identity.API registers no external auth handlers, unknown schemes throw at challenge time, and the provider label is read from a server-set temp cookie; exploitation requires hypothetical future code.

findings.title: Diagnostics endpoint dumps all session claims and cookie properties behind an unreliable localhost IP check
findings.description: DiagnosticsController.Index (lines 13-17) gates solely on RemoteIpAddress in {127.0.0.1, ::1, LocalIpAddress}; in containerized/platform deployments traffic may arrive with loopback-adjacent source addresses. Diagnostics/Index.cshtml:16-37 renders the authenticated user's full claim set and authentication-cookie property items - everything ProfileService emits (card_number, card_security_number, address, email, phone - see F-005). Scoring caveat: the controller is [Authorize], so the viewer sees their own claims, and RemoteIpAddress is socket-level rather than remotely forgeable via HTTP headers in the default middleware configuration (forwarded-header rewriting is governed by F-058).
findings.exploit_scenario: In a deployment where the reverse proxy/sidecar presents loopback-adjacent source IPs, a user opening /Diagnostics reads their complete claim payload, including card data, in cleartext HTML; combined with F-058's blanket forwarded-headers enablement, a spoofed X-Forwarded-For can pass the IP gate for an authenticated caller.
findings.recommendation: Disable the diagnostics controller in non-development environments (environment gate like HomeController.Index), and never render raw authentication properties/token items.
findings.confidence_reason: [Authorize]-gated showing the user their own claims with no remotely-forgeable IP path under default middleware - inherited sample boilerplate, missing-hardening only (pairs with F-058 for the forwarded-header angle).

findings.title: Outbox events stranded in InProgress/Failed states are never republished - broker fault injection silently kills events
findings.description: RetrieveEventLogsPendingToPublishAsync (lines 19-32) only returns entries with `State == EventStateEnum.NotPublished` filtered by the current transactionId, and TransactionBehavior calls it exactly once per command with that same transactionId (src/Ordering.API/Application/Behaviors/TransactionBehavior.cs:49-52). OrderingIntegrationEventService marks an entry InProgress before publishing (OrderingIntegrationEventService.cs:23) and Failed on error (line 31); there is no recovery job anywhere in the codebase that retries InProgress/PublishedFailed entries. A crash between MarkEventAsInProgressAsync and PublishAsync (line 24) - or a publish failure at that instant - strands the event forever, breaking the outbox's at-least-once guarantee.
findings.exploit_scenario: An actor with network control triggers a connection reset right after a legitimate order commits; the committed transaction's integration events are marked InProgress, the publish never lands, and since no job re-scans InProgress rows the order proceeds without downstream effects (basket keeps items, stock never reserved).
findings.recommendation: Add a background sweeper that re-publishes NotPublished (by any transaction) and InProgress entries older than a threshold, with publish-side idempotency keyed on EventId; treat PublishedFailed as retryable with backoff.
findings.confidence_reason: Mechanics verified (NotPublished+transactionId filter, InProgress then publish, no retry job), but this is a known outbox resiliency gap requiring attacker-controlled network disruption to weaponize - reliability finding, not an exploitable vulnerability.

findings.title: Postgres superuser credentials with weak placeholder password checked in across five services' config
findings.description: Five checked-in appsettings.Development.json files carry the identical superuser connection string with password 'yourWeak(!)Password': src/Ordering.API/appsettings.Development.json:3, src/Identity.API/appsettings.Development.json:3, src/Catalog.API/appsettings.Development.json:3, src/Webhooks.API/appsettings.Development.json:10, src/OrderProcessor/appsettings.Development.json:10 (user `postgres`, host `localhost`). .config/CredScanSuppressions.json:9-11 suppresses this placeholder from credential scanning. The pattern encourages copy-paste reuse of the weak superuser password when templating real deployments.
findings.exploit_scenario: An operator stages a production database using the development file as reference (or runs services with ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Development), leaving a publicly-known 'yourWeak(!)Password' superuser credential on the database; attacker reaches postgres and gets full read/write over Identity/Ordering/Catalog data.
findings.recommendation: Keep connection strings out of the repo entirely (user-secrets/env in dev); rotate any DB deployed with this password; remove the CredScan suppression so regressions are caught.
findings.confidence_reason: Placeholder 'yourWeak(!)Password' in Development-only files for localhost matches the dev-only-config false-positive pattern (deliberately non-real value, CredScan-suppressed); risk is purely a copy-into-prod hypothetical.

findings.title: Circuit-bound identity snapshots: ChatState captures the user principal once and user-scoped calls ride a token resolved from ambient HttpContext
findings.description: Chatbot.razor builds ChatState once at component init with `auth.User` from AuthenticationStateProvider (Chatbot.razor:106-107); ChatState holds `_user` for the lifetime of the circuit (ChatState.cs:13, 99). Meanwhile all user-scoped backing calls (basket gRPC, catalog, ordering) resolve their bearer token per-send from `IHttpContextAccessor.HttpContext` (HttpClientExtensions.cs:36-46), which on a Blazor Server circuit may be null or stale; no RevalidatingServerAuthenticationStateProvider is registered (Extensions.cs:90), and BasketState caches the fetched basket per circuit (BasketState.cs:15, 117-119). A long-lived chat circuit can keep answering GetUserInfo/GetCartContents for the principal captured at connect time after logout. Scoring caveat: the shared-machine scenario largely collapses in practice - logout via the OIDC flow ends the navigation context, and a stale IHttpContextAccessor on circuits typically yields a null token that fails closed.
findings.exploit_scenario: User signs in on a shared machine, opens the chat panel, walks away; a colleague triggers logout and signs in as a different user - if the circuit survives enhanced navigation, the still-alive ChatState answers account/cart questions from the first user's claims/basket.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the current principal per message send rather than capturing it in ChatState; subscribe to AuthenticationStateChanged to rebuild/discard chat state; validate the token is still current before each user-scoped tool call.
findings.confidence_reason: Circuit-captured principal and IHttpContextAccessor-token resolution accurately described, but the shared-machine scenario collapses in practice - stale accessor typically yields null tokens that fail closed rather than leaking.

findings.title: SaveTokens persists the IdP access token inside the auth cookie, which the relay then distributes to every backend
findings.description: Line 80 sets options.SaveTokens = true (no offline_access scope is requested, so no refresh token, but the raw IdP access token and id_token are stored in AuthenticationProperties serialized into the encrypted session cookie - cookie lifetime at line 71, default 60 minutes). HttpClientAuthorizationDelegatingHandler (src/eShop.ServiceDefaults/HttpClientExtensions.cs:38-44) extracts that token via GetTokenAsync("access_token") and attaches it to every call on the three typed clients (basket gRPC, catalog, ordering). Because audience validation is disabled fleet-wide (F-024) the cookie-embedded token is a universal credential. The cookie is protected by DataProtection encryption, which is what keeps this LOW.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker who recovers one victim's WebApp session cookie (via any adjacent app-layer bug or mis-scoped logging of request headers) replays the embedded access token directly against ordering-api and basket-api, impersonating the user fleet-wide.
findings.recommendation: Disable SaveTokens, or store tokens server-side keyed by session id; at minimum strip the access token from cookie-serialized properties and keep it in a short-lived server cache.
findings.confidence_reason: SaveTokens=true confirmed but it is standard OIDC client practice storing tokens in a DataProtection-encrypted cookie; the only 'exploit' is possessing the session itself, which grants the same access anyway - design choice.

findings.title: Unauthenticated MapForwarder relays attacker-shaped {id} into the catalog-api request path
findings.description: app.MapForwarder("/product-images/{id}", "https+http://catalog-api", "/api/catalog/items/{id}/pic") proxies public traffic to catalog-api with the route value interpolated into the destination path, with no RequireAuthorization on the mapped route and no request-path constraint on {id}. If the forwarder path transform interpolates the decoded route value without re-encoding, segment payloads such as %2E%2E-style sequences could escape the /items/{id}/pic layout. Scoring caveats: whether YARP re-encodes interpolated route values in this transform mode is unverified, and the impact floor is confirmed - the destination is pinned to catalog-api where all endpoints (per F-003, no Authorize/FallbackPolicy anywhere) are already anonymous, so traversal buys almost nothing.
findings.exploit_scenario: Attacker requests /product-images/%2e%2e%2fsome%5fother%5froute against WebApp; if the transform splices the decoded value, catalog-api receives a path outside the /pic layout - but every reachable catalog-api route is already public.
findings.recommendation: Add an int/regex route constraint to {id}, and ensure the YARP transform URL-encodes route values when constructing the destination path; separately, Catalog.API should register authentication (F-003).
findings.confidence_reason: The unauthenticated forwarder without route constraints is real, but YARP's route-value re-encoding is unverified and the impact floor is confirmed - destination endpoints are already anonymous, so traversal buys almost nothing.

findings.title: sub-less access tokens create subscriptions owned by NULL user id, forming a shared pseudo-tenant namespace
findings.description: user.GetUserId() returns principal.FindFirst("sub")?.Value and is nullable (eShop.ServiceDefaults/ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:8). WebHooksApi assigns it without any guard: POST stores UserId = user.GetUserId() (WebHooksApi.cs:51), and GET/DELETE filter with s.UserId == userId (WebHooksApi.cs:16,27,72) where userId is null for any token lacking a sub claim. All such principals would share one null-keyed namespace: each sees, modifies, and deletes every other sub-less principal's subscriptions - including their Tokens (returned in full by GET /, WebHooksApi.cs:17, and GET /{id}, line 30). Scoring caveat: no in-repo flow yields a sub-less token - identity-api issues Code/Implicit user tokens and AddAuthToken forwards user tokens - so the exploit chain depends on a token type the deployment cannot produce as configured.
findings.exploit_scenario: A service obtains a machine token (client-credentials, no sub claim) and registers subscriptions; it can then enumerate the tokens/DestUrls registered by other sub-less machine principals via GET /api/webhooks and delete their hooks via DELETE /{id}.
findings.recommendation: Reject tokens without a sub claim in the subscription endpoints (return 401/400), and add a filter predicate ensuring userId is non-null before querying/storing.
findings.confidence_reason: Unguarded nullable GetUserId() and null-compensated EF filters confirmed (UserId column is nullable in the migration), but no in-repo flow yields a sub-less token - exploit chain depends on a token type the deployment cannot produce.

findings.title: Attacker-settable stored PictureFileName is resolved to a file with no format allowlist; served MIME type is derived from the attacker-chosen extension
findings.description: The 913acea fix is verified sound: PhysicalFileProvider (Microsoft.Extensions.FileProviders.Physical 10.0.x) trims leading separators, rejects rooted paths, rejects net-negative '..' depth and enforces containment with a trailing-slash-normalized Root prefix - no regression or bypass found in the picture endpoint (lines 251-273) or any sibling file-resolution path. Residual gaps that remain exploitable-by-chain: (1) PictureFileName is a free-form attacker-controlled string - settable via anonymous PUT body (CurrentValues.SetValues, line 390) and POST (line 425) with no validation - and is resolved against the Pics root (line 263), so an attacker can point any item's picture at any of the 101 Pics files; safety rests entirely on the third-party library's confinement. (2) The served Content-Type is derived from that attacker-chosen extension via GetImageMimeTypeFromImageFileExtension (lines 269-270, 455-467), including .svg -> image/svg+xml and .wmf -> image/wmf; TypedResults.File serves bytes inline. Currently no endpoint in this service writes attacker bytes into Pics (all content is repo-shipped .webp), so the content-type confusion/stored-SVG chain is latent, not live.
findings.exploit_scenario: Step 1 (live today): anonymously PUT an item with PictureFileName "101.webp" and harvest any Pics-resident file. Step 2 (requires any future attacker-writable path into Pics): POST an item with PictureFileName "payload.svg" whose content is script markup and have victim browsers execute it when the storefront loads /product-images/* for that item.
findings.recommendation: Validate PictureFileName against a strict allowlist at write time (e.g. regex ^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+\.webp$) and/or resolve against the provider and require the resolved name to equal the stored one; remove .svg/.wmf from the extension-to-MIME map or serve with content-disposition.
findings.confidence_reason: Code facts accurate (free-form PictureFileName, extension-derived MIME incl. .svg) but the finding concedes the traversal fix is sound and exploitation requires a hypothetical future attacker-writable Pics path - latent/missing-hardening-only.

findings.title: Database connection string with password committed to source control (identitydb Development config)
findings.description: appsettings.Development.json line 3 commits `"IdentityDB": "Host=localhost;Database=IdentityDB;Username=postgres;Password=yourWeak(!)Password"`. The value looks like a template placeholder, and deployments inject real connection strings via Aspire/compose env - it establishes the pattern that identity-store credentials live in committed files, and any real deployment that forgot to override it runs the identity database on a superuser account with this password.
findings.exploit_scenario: If an environment inherits this file without override, an attacker reaching postgres:5432 authenticates as postgres with the committed password and dumps/edits the AspNetUsers table (password hashes, card data, security stamps).
findings.recommendation: Move connection strings to user-secrets/environment variables and remove committed passwords; ensure the identity DB account is not a superuser.
findings.confidence_reason: The string is verbatim in the file, but 'yourWeak(!)Password' is an obvious placeholder in a Development-only file (deployments inject real connection strings via Aspire/compose env) - fitting the env-var/template-credential false-positive pattern.

findings.title: Unauthenticated OPTIONS /check reflects arbitrary attacker header value into the response header
findings.description: The anonymous OPTIONS /check handler copies the attacker-controlled X-eshop-whtoken request-header value verbatim into the response via response.Headers.Append(webhookCheckHeader, value) (WebhookEndpoints.cs:20-23). Kestrel rejects CR/LF/NUL in inbound header values and HttpHeaders.Append validates values, so classic CRLF response-splitting is likely blocked by the framework; residual risk is reflecting otherwise-odd header content (e.g., obs-text bytes permitted end-to-end) and caching layers storing poisoned variants.
findings.exploit_scenario: Attacker sends OPTIONS /check with X-eshop-whtoken containing allowed-but-hostile ASCII; the value appears in the response headers unfiltered - meaningful mainly if a CDN/cache or intermediary mishandles the echoed value.
findings.recommendation: Instead of echoing the received value, reply with a fixed sentinel (e.g., the configured token only when validation passes), or validate the reflected value against the expected token format before appending.
findings.confidence_reason: Reflection confirmed but CR/LF rejected at both Kestrel ingress and HttpHeaders validation; the value echoes only to the requester on an unauthenticated probe - residual cache-poisoning theory, near noise.

findings.title: DEBUG build ships an extra trusted issuer "https://10.0.2.2:5243"
findings.description: Lines 42-47: under #if DEBUG, ValidIssuers includes "https://10.0.2.2:5243" (Android-emulator convenience). If Debug binaries drift into a deployed environment (image built from a debug configuration), services accept tokens whose iss is that address. Scoring caveat: JwtBearer still validates signatures against keys from the configured Authority (identityUrl), so a rogue IdP at that address cannot mint accepted tokens - only the issuer-string check is relaxed, and only in debug builds.
findings.exploit_scenario: Compromised pod in a Debug-built deployment obtains/holds a key from the real JWKS and presents tokens with iss=https://10.0.2.2:5243; the issuer check alone would not have blocked this variant.
findings.recommendation: Remove the 10.0.2.2 issuer from source; derive it from configuration so only intentional dev environments can activate it, and assert IsDevelopment() before adding.
findings.confidence_reason: Code is as described (DEBUG-only ValidIssuers with 10.0.2.2:5243), but the exploit overstates impact - JwtBearer still validates signatures against the configured Authority's keys, so a rogue IdP at that address cannot mint accepted tokens; only the issuer-string check is relaxed, in debug builds only.
